name: Pear
summary: Pear is rare in the Philippines: there are no pear farms, only a few hobby trees in cool highland gardens in Baguio and Benguet and some trees raised from seed elsewhere that seldom fruit. This short guide is for highland growers trying low chill pear types.
season: Trees are planted at the start of the rains, about May to July, in the highlands. Without a winter, growers use the same tricks as for apple: stripping leaves and bending branches to bring on flowers.
material: Grafted trees of low chill pear types from a specialty nursery. Trees from the seeds of store pears grow but take many years and seldom bear good fruit.
water: Rain fed, with watering in dry spells. Never in standing water.
fertilizer: Compost, rotted manure and small amounts of complete fertilizer (14 14 14).
care: Branch bending, leaf stripping after each crop, light pruning, bagging fruit against flies.
harvest: Fruit is picked when it lifts off with a twist. Asian types ripen on the tree, other types soften after picking.

ways.label: Grafted trees (grafted na punla)

steps.title: Choose cool, sunny ground
steps.how: Pick the coolest sunny spot you have, where water drains. Dig holes about 50 cm wide and deep with rotted manure or compost.

parts.title: Lay out the holes
parts.how: Stake the planting spots about 4 by 4 m apart, wider for big, spreading types.

parts.title: Dig and keep the soils apart
parts.how: Dig each hole about 50 cm square and 60 cm deep, piling the dark topsoil on one side and the paler subsoil on the other. Break up the hard bottom with an iron bar.

parts.title: Mix the subsoil
parts.how: Into the subsoil, mix about 500 g of agricultural lime, chicken manure or compost, about half a kerosene can, and about 500 g of complete fertilizer (14 14 14).

parts.title: Fill the hole in two layers
parts.how: Put the mixed subsoil into the hole first and the topsoil over it, then open a small hole in the middle for the tree.

parts.title: Keep the bud union high
parts.how: When you plant, trim off broken roots, bury the tree only as deep as it sat in its bag, and keep the graft joint at least 15 cm above the soil. Crumble fine soil around the roots and tramp it firm.

steps.title: Plant at the start of the rains
steps.how: Set the grafted tree at the same depth, graft joint above the soil, about 4 m apart. Firm, water, stake and mulch.

steps.title: Bend the long branches
steps.how: Tie long upright branches down toward level so they form flower buds. Feed compost and a little complete fertilizer (14 14 14) every few months.

parts.title: Choose young branches full of buds
parts.how: Pick branches one to two years old that carry many sleeping buds along their length.

parts.title: Pull them down level
parts.how: Bend each one gently out to the side until it lies flat, at a right angle to the trunk, and tie its tip with straw rope to a peg driven into the ground.

parts.title: Let the spurs form
parts.how: Buds on the upper side of the bent branch push out shoots, and most of them stay short as fruiting spurs that flower the following year.

steps.title: Strip leaves after growth stops
steps.how: Pick off the mature leaves by hand to push new flowers and leaves, and repeat after each crop.

parts.title: Strip every leaf from the bent branches
parts.how: When growth has stopped and the leaves are mature, pick off all the leaves on the bent branches by hand. It takes the place of the cold the highlands do not give.

parts.title: Watch for flowers in about three weeks
parts.how: About three weeks after bending and stripping, the flower buds at the branch tips open and new shoots start from the sleeping buds.

steps.title: Pick mature fruit
steps.how: We count the first crop at about 48 months. Pick when the fruit lifts off easily with a twist and the skin color lightens.

ways.note: We count the first harvest at about 48 months (1,440 days). Many trees here bear little.

mistakes: Growing pears from store seeds and waiting for fruit that seldom comes.
Planting high chill types that need a cold winter.
better: Buy grafted low chill types and plant only in cool highlands.
Bend branches and strip leaves on a schedule, and keep notes.
Test the soil and feed by the result.

watering.traditional: The few pear trees here, in the highlands, live on rain with a pail of water in dry spells, on ground where water never stands.
watering.method: A pail or hose into a ring basin around the tree, in the morning.
watering.rainfed: Plant as the rains begin on cool, sunny, well drained high ground and mulch the ring. Rain carries the tree, with a pail of water in dry spells while it flowers and fills fruit.
watering.dryseason: Water when the soil a hand deep is dry, most of all from leaf stripping to fruit growth.
watering.wet: Pears must never stand in water: plant on slopes or mounds and keep drains open.

schedule.often: Soak at planting, then whenever the soil dries in a dry spell, until the tree is clearly growing
schedule.amount: A good soak of the mulched ring around the stem
schedule.why: The roots are still in the bag ball and the tree is not yet established.

schedule.often: Only in dry spells, when the soil a hand deep is dry
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring, never leaving water standing
schedule.why: These trees grow in cool, wet uplands, where rain usually covers them.

schedule.stage: Leaf stripping to new shoots and flowers (each crop cycle)
schedule.often: Keep the soil moist after stripping the leaves. Water if a dry spell comes
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring under the leaves
schedule.why: New shoots and flowers push out in the weeks after stripping.

schedule.stage: Flowering to four weeks after bloom
schedule.often: Never let the soil dry out
schedule.amount: A deep soak whenever the soil a hand deep is dry
schedule.why: Stress now cuts fruit set and final fruit size.

schedule.stage: Fruit growth to harvest (first real crop)
schedule.often: Steady water in dry spells up to picking
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring
schedule.why: The fruits swell over the last weeks and stay small if the soil dries.

critical: Flowering to about four weeks after bloom.
The last weeks of fruit growth before picking.

signs.dry: Leaves droop and brown at the edges, few fruits set, and fruits stay small.
signs.wet: Yellow leaves and rotting roots on soggy ground.

better: Keep the soil steadily moist from leaf stripping until four weeks after bloom, and in the last weeks before picking.
